Content:
Factorials can be applied to variables, too. To manipulate a factorial expression involving a variable, we just need to remember that the variable represents a number, and the previous number can be obtained by subtracting [MATH: 1] from the variable.

Content:
So, in the same way that we have

Content:
[MATH: 5!|= 5 ⋅ 4 ⋅ 3 ⋅ 2 ⋅ 1^(⏞)^(4!); = 5 ⋅ 4!]

Content:
we also have

Content:
[MATH: n!|= n ⋅ (n − 1) ⋅ (n − 2) ⋅ ⋯ ⋅ 2 ⋅ 1^(⏞)^((n − 1)!); = n ⋅ (n − 1)!]

Content:
where [MATH: n] denotes some positive integer.

Content:
Likewise, in the same way that we have

Content:
[MATH: 5! = 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3!]

Content:
we also have

Content:
[MATH: x! = x \cdot (x-1) \cdot (x-2)!]

items.title: Writing a Factorial in an Equivalent Form

sections.normalized_html:
Which of the following is equivalent to [MATH: (k+1)!] for any [MATH: k \geq 2?]

  1. [MATH: (k+1) \cdot k \cdot (k-1)]

  2. [MATH: (k+1) \cdot k \cdot (k-1)!]

  3. [MATH: (k+1) \cdot k]
sections.readable_text:
Which of the following is equivalent to [MATH: (k+1)!] for any [MATH: k \geq 2?]

1. [MATH: (k+1) \cdot k \cdot (k-1)]
2. [MATH: (k+1) \cdot k \cdot (k-1)!]
3. [MATH: (k+1) \cdot k]

sections.normalized_html:
Using the definition of factorial, we have

[MATH: (k+1)! = (k+1) \cdot k \cdot (k-1) \cdot (k-2) \cdot \: \cdots \: \cdot 2 \cdot 1.]

Now, applying the factorial definition to all but the first two factors, we get

[MATH: (k + 1)!|= (k + 1) ⋅ k ⋅ (k − 1) ⋅ (k − 2) ⋅ ⋯ ⋅ 2 ⋅ 1^(⏞)^((k − 1)!); = (k + 1) ⋅ k ⋅ (k − 1)!]

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

items.title: Simplifying a Variable Expression Containing a Quotient of Factorials

sections.normalized_html: Given that [MATH: n \geq 2] is an integer, simplify [MATH: \dfrac {n!} {(n - 2)!}.]
sections.readable_text: Given that [MATH: n \geq 2] is an integer, simplify [MATH: \dfrac {n!} {(n - 2)!}.]

sections.normalized_html:
First, notice the following:

[MATH: n! = n \cdot (n-1) \cdot (n-2)!]

Then, we cancel the [MATH: (n-2)!] that occurs in both the numerator and the denominator:

[MATH: \eqalign{ \dfrac {n!} {(n - 2)!} &= \dfrac {n \cdot (n - 1) \cdot (n - 2)!} {(n - 2)!}\[5pt] &= \dfrac {n \cdot (n - 1) \cdot \cancel{(n - 2)!}} {\cancel{(n - 2)!}}\[5pt] &= n(n -1) \[5pt] &= n^2 - n }]

sections.normalized_html: Given that [MATH: k \geq 1] is an integer, simplify [MATH: \dfrac {k^2(k - 1)!} {k!}.]
sections.readable_text: Given that [MATH: k \geq 1] is an integer, simplify [MATH: \dfrac {k^2(k - 1)!} {k!}.]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we notice that

[MATH: k! = k \cdot (k-1)!]

So, we can simplify the numerator as follows:

[MATH: k^2 (k-1)! = k \cdot \underbrace{k \cdot (k-1)!}_{k!} = k \cdot k!]

Then, we cancel the [MATH: k!] that occurs in both the numerator and the denominator:

[MATH: \eqalign{ \dfrac {k^2(k - 1)!} {k!} &= \dfrac {k \cdot k!} {k!}\[5pt] &= \dfrac {k \cdot \cancel{k!}} {\cancel{k!}} \[5pt] &= \dfrac {k} {1} \[5pt] &= k }]

Item 2 — Example: Writing a Factorial in an Equivalent Form

Item 5 — Example: Simplifying a Variable Expression Containing a Quotient of Factorials

Example Prompt:
Given that [MATH: n \geq 2] is an integer, simplify [MATH: \dfrac {n!} {(n - 2)!}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, notice the following:

[MATH: n! = n \cdot (n-1) \cdot (n-2)!]

Then, we cancel the [MATH: (n-2)!] that occurs in both the numerator and the denominator:

[MATH: \eqalign{
\dfrac {n!} {(n - 2)!}
&= \dfrac {n \cdot (n - 1) \cdot (n - 2)!} {(n - 2)!}\[5pt]

&= \dfrac {n \cdot (n - 1) \cdot \cancel{(n - 2)!}} {\cancel{(n - 2)!}}\[5pt]

&= n(n -1) \[5pt]
&= n^2 - n
}]
